note: AI-drafted. New records were researched from fetched pages and fact-checked a second time. Link proposals were drafted against the full record text and are unconfirmed.

newRecords.title: ACM, Code.org, CSTA, Cyber Innovation Center and NMSI launch the K-12 Computer Science Framework
newRecords.summary: Five organizations released a framework that describes core computer science concepts and practices for K-12 students and how understanding grows over time. It was written with states, districts and the computer science education community to guide the development of standards and curriculum.
newRecords.notes: Primary here means the framework developers' own press release. The source is a standards-body page and no government agency issued it.

newRecords.title: Computer Science Teachers Association publishes the revised CSTA K-12 Computer Science Standards
newRecords.summary: The Computer Science Teachers Association published a revised set of K-12 computer science standards aligned to the 2016 K-12 Computer Science Framework. The revision updated the association's first comprehensive standards, released in 2011.
newRecords.notes: The CSTA page gives only the year. Primary here means the standards body's own page; CSTA standards are voluntary guidance that states may adopt.

newRecords.title: Computer Science Teachers Association publishes the 2026 PK-12 Computer Science Standards
newRecords.summary: CSTA published its 2026 PK-12 computer science standards. A writing team of 25 people from 18 states finalized them in spring 2026. The set has foundational standards from pre-kindergarten through grade 12 and high school specialty standards in six areas.
newRecords.notes: The page places publication in summer 2026 without a day. The six specialty areas come from the CSTA standards landing page https://csteachers.org/pk12standards/ which I also fetched.

newRecords.title: Every Student Succeeds Act becomes law and lists computer science in the federal definition of a well-rounded education
newRecords.issuingBody: United States Congress and the President
newRecords.summary: The Every Student Succeeds Act (Public Law 114-95) names computer science among the subjects in the federal definition of a well-rounded education. States and local school districts may add further subjects to that list.
newRecords.notes: Cornell LII reproduces 20 U.S.C. 7801(52), added by Pub. L. 114-95 sec. 8002(21). The approval date of December 10, 2015 for Pub. L. 114-95 (S. 1177) was confirmed on https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-114publ95/html/PLAW-114publ95.htm, but I could not reach the definition itself on that page because the page text was truncated.

newRecords.title: President directs the Education Department to prioritize STEM and computer science in grant making
newRecords.summary: A presidential memorandum told the Secretary of Education to make high-quality STEM education, with a focus on computer science, a Department priority when awarding grants from fiscal year 2018. It set a goal of at least $200 million a year in grant funds and asked for guidance on computer science education.
newRecords.notes: Published in the Federal Register on September 28, 2017. The memorandum applies to the extent consistent with law and subject to appropriations.

newRecords.title: President issues Executive Order 14277 on advancing artificial intelligence education for American youth
newRecords.summary: The order creates a White House Task Force on AI Education and a Presidential AI Challenge. It directs federal agencies to develop online K-12 AI literacy resources, calls for Education Department guidance on using grant funds for AI in instruction, and gives priority to AI in teacher training and high school AI courses.
newRecords.notes: The executive order number 14277 appears in the fetched page summary and in govinfo search results.

newRecords.title: US Department of Education issues guidance on using federal grant funds for AI and proposes an AI grant priority
newRecords.summary: The Department sent state and district leaders a Dear Colleague letter saying federal grant funds may be used for AI in curriculum tools, tutoring and career advising. It also proposed a grant priority for AI projects, which includes AI literacy in lessons and educator training in computer science and AI foundations.
newRecords.notes: K-12 Dive reports the letter on Tuesday July 22, 2025 and a proposed rule in the Federal Register on July 21, 2025. The ed.gov press release returned an access error so the primary text was not read. The proposed priority was open for comment, and its final status is unconfirmed.

newRecords.title: NY Board of Regents adopts the first K-12 Computer Science and Digital Fluency Learning Standards
newRecords.issuingBody: New York State Board of Regents
newRecords.summary: The Regents adopted New York's first K-12 learning standards for computer science and digital fluency, organized into five concepts and grade bands from K-1 to 9-12. The state roadmap sets full implementation across all grade bands from September 2024.
newRecords.notes: The release URL carries 2023 and its roll-out table starts at August 2021, but the dateline reads December 14, 2020 and the NYSED roadmap https://www.nysed.gov/sites/default/files/programs/standards-instruction/nys-csdf-standards-timeline-and-roadmap.pdf says December 2020.

newRecords.title: NY Board of Regents conditionally approves the first Computer Science and Digital Fluency Learning Standards
newRecords.summary: The Regents gave conditional approval to New York's first learning standards for computer science and digital fluency. The kindergarten to grade 2 standards needed more work with early learning experts, and the full set was to return to the Board later in 2020 for final adoption.
newRecords.notes: Some URLs for this NYSED release carry 2025 in the path, but the dateline on the fetched page reads January 13, 2020.

newRecords.title: California enacts AB 1539 asking for K-12 computer science content standards
newRecords.summary: AB 1539 (Chapter 876, Statutes of 2014) added Education Code section 60605.4. It asks the Instructional Quality Commission to consider developing and recommending K-12 computer science content standards to the State Board by July 31, 2019. Districts may use the standards, and the work depends on funding being appropriated.
newRecords.notes: The status page https://www.leginfo.ca.gov/pub/13-14/bill/asm/ab_1501-1550/ab_1539_bill_20140930_status.html also lists chaptering by the Secretary of State on September 30, 2014.

newRecords.title: California State Board of Education adopts the state's first K-12 computer science standards
newRecords.summary: The State Board of Education approved California's first computer science standards for K-12 students. They cover core computer science concepts, such as algorithms and programming, and core practices, such as creating computational artifacts.
newRecords.notes: The California Department of Education pages blocked automated access, so the primary page was not read. The article is dated September 13, 2018.

newRecords.title: California enacts AB 2876 on AI literacy in school curriculum frameworks
newRecords.summary: AB 2876 (Chapter 927, Statutes of 2024) asks the Instructional Quality Commission to consider adding AI literacy content to the mathematics, science and history-social science frameworks when they are next revised after January 1, 2025. It also asks the Commission to consider AI literacy when evaluating instructional materials for those subjects.
newRecords.notes: The date is the chaptering date shown on the bill tracker. The page does not state the Governor's approval date, and the official leginfo page returned an access error.

newRecords.title: Florida enacts CS/HB 495 with requirements for K-12 computer science instruction
newRecords.summary: CS/HB 495 (Chapter 2018-150) is a K-12 public education bill that includes requirements for specified computer science instruction and cites section 1007.2616, Florida Statutes. The Governor approved it on April 6, 2018, and it took effect July 1, 2018.
newRecords.notes: The bill page does not spell out the requirements. The current text of section 1007.2616 (read at leg.state.fl.us) has public schools give K-12 students chances to learn computer science, with computer science courses in middle and high school.

newRecords.title: Florida State Board of Education publishes notice to update the state computer science standards
newRecords.summary: The Department of Education published a notice of rule development for amendments to Rule 6A-1.09401, Student Performance Standards. The stated purpose was to update Florida's state academic standards for computer science. A rule development workshop was set for June 12, 2024.
newRecords.notes: The workshop date comes from the register PDF https://flrules.org/faw/fawdocuments/fawvolumefolders2024/50104/50104doc.pdf, which I read.

newRecords.title: Florida State Board of Education rule listing the 2024 computer science standards takes effect
newRecords.summary: Rule 6A-1.09401, Student Performance Standards, took effect in an amended form on August 27, 2024. Its reference list includes Florida's State Academic Standards for Computer Science, 2024. The July 2, 2024 version of the same rule listed no computer science standards.
newRecords.notes: The Board vote date was not confirmed from a fetched page. A July 24, 2024 Board agenda item appears only in search results. Cornell LII's copy of the rule also lists the 2024 computer science standards and an amendment effective 8/27/2024.

newRecords.title: Florida State Board of Education begins rulemaking on K-12 course requirements including computer science courses
newRecords.summary: A notice of rule development for Rule 6A-1.09412, Course Requirements for Grades K-12, said the amendments would include changes to requirements for K-12 computer science courses. The amended rule took effect on December 24, 2024.
newRecords.notes: The December 24, 2024 effective date comes from final notice https://www.flrules.org/gateway/View_notice.asp?id=29042593, which lists a Computer Science reference document but does not describe the changes.

newRecords.title: Pennsylvania State Board of Education approves a resolution endorsing the CSTA K-12 Computer Science Standards
newRecords.summary: The State Board of Education approved a resolution endorsing the K-12 computer science standards developed by the Computer Science Teachers Association. The Board's archive lists the action under January 11, 2018.
newRecords.notes: This is an endorsement resolution. The Board's page of academic standards published in the Pennsylvania Bulletin (https://www.pa.gov/agencies/stateboard/resources/regulations--policy/state-academic-standards.html) lists no computer science set. The archive shows titles only, so the resolution text was not read.

newRecords.title: Pennsylvania Department of Education approves the Framework for Computer Science 7-12 Program Guidelines
newRecords.summary: The Pennsylvania Department of Education developed and approved a framework of program guidelines for computer science in grades 7 to 12 in December 2018. The same department page records the State Board's January 2018 endorsement of the CSTA standards.
newRecords.notes: The page gives the month only and does not link a document I could read.

newRecords.title: Tennessee State Board of Education gives final approval to the state's first K-8 computer science standards
newRecords.summary: The State Board gave final approval to Tennessee's first computer science standards for elementary and middle schools. They replaced computer technology standards last revised in 2011, and the benchmarks were set to reach classrooms in fall 2019.
newRecords.notes: The Tri-State Defender repost names Friday, July 27, 2018. The Chalkbeat original at https://www.chalkbeat.org:443/tennessee/2018/7/27/21107006/tennessee-approves-its-first-ever-computer-science-standards-for-k-8-schools is dated July 27, 2018 and gives the 2011 and fall 2019 details. Tennessee Department of Education pages blocked automated access.

newRecords.title: Tennessee General Assembly passes Public Chapter 979 setting computer science requirements for K-12 schools
newRecords.summary: Public Chapter 979 of 2022 passed the General Assembly unanimously. Elementary schools give each student grade-appropriate computer science education, middle schools provide computer science for at least one grading period, and high school students on a traditional diploma earn at least one computer science credit.
newRecords.notes: Only the year is confirmed from a fetched page. The Tennessee Code section 49-1-307 text (FindLaw, https://codes.findlaw.com/tn/title-49-education/tn-code-sect-49-1-307/) has the State Board adopt computer science standards, available for 2023-2024 and required from 2024-2025, but I could not confirm from a fetched page that Public Chapter 979 enacted it. Official Tennessee sites blocked automated access. Sources differ on whether middle-school students must take the course or only have access to it.

newRecords.title: National Council for the Social Studies releases the C3 Framework for state social studies standards
newRecords.issuingBody: National Council for the Social Studies (NCSS)
newRecords.summary: NCSS and partner organizations released the College, Career, and Civic Life (C3) Framework, guidance for states that are revising their social studies standards. It covers civics, economics, geography and history and is organized around an inquiry approach to teaching.
newRecords.notes: The CIRCLE post and an American Historical Association article are both dated 17 September 2013, but Education Week says the document went online the week before, so only the month is given. NCSS's own page could not be fetched.

newRecords.title: Congress enacts the Every Student Succeeds Act, which authorizes a federal American history and civics education program
newRecords.summary: The Every Student Succeeds Act (Public Law 114-95) was approved on December 10, 2015. In Title II, sections 2231 to 2233 authorize the Secretary of Education to run an American history and civics education program, including Presidential and Congressional Academies and national grant activities.
newRecords.notes: Read in the enacted public law text on govinfo (approval line: December 10, 2015). The record covers only this one program. It leaves out the rest of the Act.

newRecords.title: Educating for American Democracy releases its Roadmap for K-12 history and civic education
newRecords.issuingBody: Educating for American Democracy (partners at iCivics, Harvard, Arizona State University and Tufts University)
newRecords.summary: A team led by iCivics, Harvard, Arizona State University and Tufts released the Roadmap to Educating for American Democracy, a framework for K-12 history and civic education built around seven themes. The project describes the themes as a starting point for designing standards, curricula and lessons. Funding came from the National Endowment for the Humanities and the US Department of Education.
newRecords.notes: ASU dates the release March 2, 2021 and the Harvard Gazette story reads as March 1, so only the month is given. The seven themes and the funding statement come from the project's own site (educatingforamericandemocracy.org/the-report/).

newRecords.title: National Assessment Governing Board launches an update of the NAEP Civics Assessment Framework
newRecords.summary: On May 15, 2026 the National Assessment Governing Board approved a charge to begin updating the NAEP Civics Assessment Framework, which would guide civics assessments from 2032. The Board also finalized plans for optional state-level results in 8th and 12th grade civics for states that opt in.
newRecords.notes: The release says subject-matter and assessment experts and an educator advisory committee will be convened and more public comment is planned.

newRecords.title: New York Board of Regents adopts the K-12 Social Studies Framework
newRecords.issuingBody: New York State Board of Regents
newRecords.summary: The Board of Regents adopted the New York State K-12 Social Studies Framework, which lists key ideas and concepts for each grade level and combines literacy skills with social studies practices. The state's five social studies standards and the kindergarten-to-grade-12 course order stay in place.
newRecords.notes: The page address contains 2015 but the release itself is dated April 29, 2014.

newRecords.title: New York State Education Department issues the revised Grades 9-12 Social Studies Framework
newRecords.summary: The State Education Department issued a revised Grades 9-12 Social Studies Framework dated February 2017. It covers Global History and Geography in grades 9 and 10, United States History and Government in grade 11, and Participation in Government and Civics and Economics in grade 12.
newRecords.notes: The cover and contents give a revision date only. The department's social studies page also lists a March 2016 revision of the K-8 framework. Whether the Regents voted on these revisions was not checked.

newRecords.title: New York Board of Regents approves the Seal of Civic Readiness and Civics Pathway for all high schools
newRecords.issuingBody: New York State Board of Regents
newRecords.summary: In September 2021 the Regents approved the Seal of Civic Readiness +1 Civics Pathway for all high schools beginning in the 2022-23 school year. A pilot with 117 schools ran in 2021-22. The Seal recognizes high civic knowledge and participation, and districts and schools apply to offer it.
newRecords.notes: Day not stated in the department manual. A May 10, 2021 department release describes the original proposal and pilot; the application detail comes from nysed.gov/curriculum-instruction/seal-civic-readiness.

newRecords.title: California State Board of Education adopts the History-Social Science Content Standards
newRecords.summary: The California State Board of Education adopted the state's history-social science content standards on October 9, 1998. A 2014 Senate bill analysis still described them as the current standards and noted that a bill (SB 1057) proposed revising them.
newRecords.notes: Date comes from an official California Senate floor analysis (August 2014). No State Board page was used because the Department of Education site blocked fetching.

newRecords.title: California State Board of Education adopts the History-Social Science Framework
newRecords.summary: The State Board adopted the History-Social Science Framework for California Public Schools, Kindergarten Through Grade Twelve, a curriculum framework with chapters for each grade or grade span. It is meant to work alongside the state's existing content standards, which are printed in an appendix.
newRecords.notes: Teacher-community site that reposts the Department of Education framework. A July 2016 local news article and a 2018 CSBA post also confirm approval in 2016 but give no exact day. The Department of Education site blocked fetching.

newRecords.title: California State Board of Education approves the Ethnic Studies Model Curriculum
newRecords.summary: The State Board approved a statewide Ethnic Studies Model Curriculum in March 2021. A later State Board letter describes it as grounded in African American, Native American, Asian/Pacific Islander American and Latinx American studies, with room for local adaptation.
newRecords.notes: The March 18 day comes from a news release quoted in the article. The 2021 adoption is also stated in an August 23, 2023 State Board letter on gov.ca.gov. Ethnic studies is a related subject within history-social science, included because it is part of the state's social studies offering.

newRecords.title: California enacts AB 101, adding an ethnic studies course to high school graduation requirements
newRecords.summary: Governor Newsom signed AB 101 on October 8, 2021. It adds a one-semester ethnic studies course as a high school graduation requirement starting with students graduating in 2029-30, and schools are to offer the course from 2025-26. The Education Code text makes the change operative only if the Legislature appropriates funds.
newRecords.notes: The 2025-26 offering date comes from an August 23, 2023 State Board letter on gov.ca.gov (Chapter 661, Statutes of 2021). The funding condition comes from a mirror of Education Code 51225.3(f) on california.public.law, so it is a secondary reading.

newRecords.title: Florida enacts HB 807 requiring a review of civics course standards and materials
newRecords.summary: CS/HB 807 (Civics Education), Chapter 2019-150, has the Commissioner of Education review civics instructional materials and test specifications and make recommendations. It also requires the Department of Education to review the statewide civics education course standards.
newRecords.notes: The Florida Senate bill page lists approval by the Governor on June 26, 2019. A 2021 House staff analysis confirms the standards review began in 2020.

newRecords.title: Florida enacts HB 5, requiring an integrated K-12 civic education curriculum
newRecords.summary: HB 5 has the Department of Education develop or approve an integrated K-12 civic education curriculum and the State Board set civic-minded expectations. It adds to U.S. Government a comparative discussion of ideologies that conflict with the founding principles of the United States, such as communism and totalitarianism, and creates the Portraits in Patriotism Act.
newRecords.notes: Source is the Florida House final bill analysis, which states that it does not reflect the sponsor's or House's official position. The Florida Senate bill page also shows Chapter 2021-158 approved 6/22/2021.

newRecords.title: Florida State Board of Education adopts revised civics and government standards and Holocaust education standards
newRecords.summary: At its July 14, 2021 meeting the State Board adopted new civics, government and Holocaust education standards, along with changes to other subjects. News reports say the civics standards call for studying primary source documents about the American republic.
newRecords.notes: CBS Miami article dated July 14, 2021; WUSF and WUFT reports of the same Wednesday meeting agree on the content. The Department of Education site blocked fetching, so no official page was read. The 2021 House bill analysis expected adoption by summer 2021.

newRecords.title: Florida State Board of Education rule 6A-1.09411 sets requirements for K-12 civic education curriculum
newRecords.summary: Rule 6A-1.09411, effective November 23, 2021, sets requirements for the integrated civic education curriculum that districts and charter schools use in grades K-12. A copy of the rule on Cornell's Legal Information Institute lists required content including the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution.
newRecords.notes: The flrules.org page shows only a summary and the history line; the list of required topics comes from law.cornell.edu/regulations/florida/Fla-Admin-Code-Ann-R-6A-1-09411. The State Board's vote date was not confirmed.

newRecords.title: Florida State Board of Education approves stand-alone K-12 African American History standards
newRecords.summary: At its July 19, 2023 meeting in Orlando the State Board approved stand-alone African American History standards for kindergarten through grade 12.
newRecords.notes: TV station report published July 19, 2023. The Florida Senate page for HB 7 (2022, Chapter 2022-72) directs the Department of Education to prepare African American history standards and curriculum. The standards drew public debate that this record does not summarize.

newRecords.title: Pennsylvania State Board of Education Chapter 4 regulation adding academic standards for civics and government, economics, geography and history takes effect
newRecords.summary: The State Board's Chapter 4 regulation (No. 6-275) added statewide academic standards in civics and government, economics, geography and history. The review commission approved the final form on November 21, 2002, and the standards took effect on publication in the Pennsylvania Bulletin on January 11, 2003.
newRecords.notes: Review dates come from the Independent Regulatory Review Commission page for Regulation 6-275 (irrc.state.pa.us/regulations/RegSrchRslts.cfm?ID=2238). The State Board's own adoption vote date was not confirmed.

newRecords.title: Pennsylvania enacts Act 35 of 2018 providing for an assessment of civic knowledge in schools
newRecords.summary: Act 35 of 2018 (House Bill 564) amends the Public School Code of 1949 to provide for an assessment of civic knowledge. School district and news pages describe a locally developed test of U.S. history, government and civics, given at least once in grades 7 to 12 beginning in 2020-21.
newRecords.notes: The legislature page gives the title, House Bill 564 and the June 19, 2018 enactment. The grade range and school year come from pasd.com/academics/assessment_information/act_35 and a Tyrone Eagle Eye News article. The act text does not state them.

newRecords.title: Pennsylvania review commission approves the State Board's updated Economics standards and new Personal Finance standards
newRecords.summary: Regulation 6-354 updates Pennsylvania's academic standards for Economics, together with Career Education and Work and Family and Consumer Sciences, and establishes new Personal Finance standards. The Independent Regulatory Review Commission approved it on December 5, 2024. The State Board lists July 1, 2026 as the effective date.
newRecords.notes: The effective date comes from the State Board standards page. That page says the standards were published in the Pennsylvania Bulletin on February 8, 2025, while the IRRC page lists publication as final on March 22, 2025, so the record uses the approval date. The State Board's own vote date was not confirmed.

newRecords.title: Tennessee State Board of Education approves new Tennessee Academic Standards for Social Studies
newRecords.summary: The State Board voted unanimously on final reading to approve new Tennessee Academic Standards for Social Studies, to be used in classrooms from the 2019-20 school year. The release says changes made after first reading responded to public feedback and to a new state law on Tennessee history.
newRecords.notes: Local news site reposting the State Board release, dated Jul 28 in the address and page. The State Board's own site could not be fetched. A Chalkbeat article of April 21, 2017 reports the earlier first-reading vote.

newRecords.title: Tennessee General Assembly passes the Senator Douglas Henry Tennessee History Act
newRecords.summary: The legislature passed a law requiring a Tennessee history course, reported as a semester, without naming a grade. Chalkbeat reported it would take effect in the 2018-19 school year. The State Board later placed the content in fifth-grade standards starting in fall 2019.
newRecords.notes: Public Chapter 482 and the Act's name come from the State Board release reposted at csenewsnow.com; the fifth-grade placement comes from a Chalkbeat article of July 26, 2017. The exact signing date was not found, so the month of final passage is given.

newRecords.title: Tennessee law begins requiring high school students to take a U.S. civics test
newRecords.summary: Under Tennessee Code 49-6-408, high school students were required from January 1, 2017 to take a civics test drawn from the 100 questions used for naturalization, with 70 percent as the passing score. Passing was optional at first. The current code makes a passing score a condition of the social studies credit for a full diploma.
newRecords.notes: Date is the start date written in the statute; the enactment date was not found. FindLaw says its copy may not show the latest version of the law, and the state sites could not be fetched.

newRecords.title: KMK adopts its declaration on media education in schools (Medienbildung in der Schule)
newRecords.titleDe: Die KMK beschließt die Erklärung „Medienbildung in der Schule“
newRecords.issuingBody: Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education (KMK)
newRecords.summary: The KMK replaces its 1995 declaration on media pedagogy. It aims to make media education a compulsory task of schooling, covering learning with media and learning about media. It lists eight fields of action, from curricula and teacher education to copyright and data protection.
newRecords.notes: The text refers to the earlier declaration 'Medienpädagogik in der Schule' of 12.05.1995. The 2016 KMK strategy states that this 2012 text remains valid.

newRecords.title: KMK adopts the strategy 'Bildung in der digitalen Welt' with a competence framework for all subjects
newRecords.titleDe: Die KMK beschließt die Strategie „Bildung in der digitalen Welt“ mit einem Kompetenzrahmen für alle Fächer
newRecords.issuingBody: Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education (KMK)
newRecords.summary: The Länder agree to build digital competences into the curricula of all subjects from primary school on and to use digital learning environments systematically. The strategy sets a framework of six competence areas. Pupils entering Grundschule or Sekundarstufe I in 2018/19 should be able to acquire them by the end of compulsory schooling.
newRecords.notes: Six areas: Suchen, Verarbeiten und Aufbewahren; Kommunizieren und Kooperieren; Produzieren und Präsentieren; Schützen und sicher Agieren; Problemlösen und Handeln; Analysieren und Reflektieren. The competences are integrated into the curricula of all subjects and no separate subject is created. The 2019 DigitalPakt agreement cites a version dated 7 December 2017; the PDF read here is the decision of 8 December 2016 in the version of 7 December 2017.

newRecords.title: KMK adopts its revised recommendation on democracy education in schools
newRecords.titleDe: Die KMK beschließt die neu gefasste Empfehlung „Demokratie als Ziel, Gegenstand und Praxis historisch-politischer Bildung und Erziehung in der Schule“
newRecords.issuingBody: Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education (KMK)
newRecords.summary: The KMK updates its 2009 recommendation. It describes the school as a place where democracy is taught and practised, bases teaching on fundamental rights and human dignity, and names the Beutelsbach Consensus with its controversy principle as a basis of democratic learning. A passage on digitalisation calls for critical media competence.
newRecords.notes: The original was adopted on 06.03.2009; this record covers the version dated 11.10.2018. The document text was read from the copy hosted by the Federal Agency for Civic Education (https://www.bpb.de/medien/278816/Beschluss_Demokratieerziehung.pdf), whose title line reads 'Beschluss der Kultusministerkonferenz vom 06.03.2009 i. d. F. vom 11.10.2018'.

newRecords.title: Federal government and the Länder sign the DigitalPakt Schule agreement worth 5 billion euros
newRecords.titleDe: Bund und Länder unterzeichnen die Verwaltungsvereinbarung DigitalPakt Schule über 5 Milliarden Euro
newRecords.issuingBody: Federal Ministry of Education and Research (BMBF) and the 16 Länder
newRecords.summary: Under Article 104c of the Basic Law, the federal government provides 5 billion euros over five years for digital infrastructure in schools. The Länder add at least 10 percent of the funded investments and pledge their own measures. The agreement takes effect the day after the last signature.
newRecords.notes: The PDF is the Bundesanzeiger notice BAnz AT 14.06.2019 B2, hosted by Rhineland-Palatinate. The signature block shows the federal minister signing in Berlin on 16 May 2019 and the Länder signing between 2 and 10 May 2019. The effective date of 17 May 2019 follows from section 20(2), which makes the agreement effective the day after the last signature.

newRecords.title: KMK adopts 'Lehren und Lernen in der digitalen Welt', a supplement to its digital education strategy
newRecords.titleDe: Die KMK beschließt die Ergänzung „Lehren und Lernen in der digitalen Welt“ zur Strategie „Bildung in der digitalen Welt“
newRecords.issuingBody: Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education (KMK)
newRecords.summary: The supplement deepens the 2016 strategy with a focus on teaching and learning. It covers pupils' competences, the potential of digital learning, examination culture, school development, digitally supported lesson design, teacher competences and teacher education. It takes in comments from an April 2021 hearing and recommendations of the SWK.
newRecords.notes: The KMK topic page for education in the digital world lists this text as a 2021 supplement to the 2016 strategy.

newRecords.title: KMK adopts revised unified Abitur examination requirements (EPA) for Informatik
newRecords.titleDe: Die KMK beschließt die neu gefassten Einheitlichen Prüfungsanforderungen in der Abiturprüfung Informatik
newRecords.issuingBody: Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education (KMK)
newRecords.summary: The EPA Informatik describe the competences and content that Abitur tasks in Informatik must cover, the three levels of task demand, and sample tasks for written and oral exams. On 12 March 2004 the KMK asked the Länder to apply the revised text by the 2007 Abitur at the latest.
newRecords.notes: The original was adopted on 01.12.1989. The KMK decisions list for general education still shows this text as its Informatik document for the Abitur, while the Biologie, Chemie and Physik EPA are marked as replaced by Bildungsstandards from the 2025 Abitur. The Informatik section of the KMK MINT page lists only EPA texts (EPA Informatik and EPA berufliche Informatik) and no Bildungsstandards. A later check could not reopen the KMK page, so the statement that Informatik has no Bildungsstandards is unconfirmed.

newRecords.title: KMK adopts revised unified Abitur examination requirements (EPA) for Sozialkunde/Politik
newRecords.titleDe: Die KMK beschließt die neu gefassten Einheitlichen Prüfungsanforderungen in der Abiturprüfung Sozialkunde/Politik
newRecords.issuingBody: Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education (KMK)
newRecords.summary: The preamble names political maturity and the capacity for democracy as guiding aims. It builds the subject on three principles (no overwhelming of pupils, controversy, pupils' interests) and on four competences: analysis, judgement, methods and action. The Länder were asked to apply the text by the 2009 Abitur at the latest.
newRecords.notes: The original was adopted on 01.12.1989. The three principles are Überwältigungsverbot, Kontroversitätsgebot and Berücksichtigung der Interessenlagen der Schülerinnen und Schüler; the four competences are Sach- und Analysekompetenz, Urteilskompetenz, Methodenkompetenz and Handlungskompetenz. A separate KMK text sets EPA for Wirtschaft (version of 16.11.2006).

newRecords.title: KMK's scientific commission (SWK) publishes its statement on democracy education in schools
newRecords.titleDe: Die Ständige Wissenschaftliche Kommission der KMK veröffentlicht die Stellungnahme „Demokratiebildung als Auftrag der Schule“
newRecords.issuingBody: Standing Scientific Commission of the KMK (SWK)
newRecords.summary: The SWK, an independent scientific advisory body of the KMK, makes seven recommendations. They call for shared competence goals and continuous teaching in Politik and Geschichte from primary school to the end of Sekundarstufe I, and for democracy education as a principle in all subjects.
newRecords.notes: This is advice to the Länder. The KMK president said in the same press release that the KMK would examine the recommendations. The full statement PDF (https://www.swk-bildung.org/content/uploads/2024/06/SWK-2024-Stellungnahme_Demokratiebildung.pdf) was also read and says it was adopted by the commission members in July 2024.

newRecords.title: KMK adopts key points for anchoring media education and informatics education in primary school
newRecords.titleDe: Die KMK beschließt das Eckpunktepapier zur Verankerung von Medienbildung und informatischer Bildung in der Grundschule
newRecords.issuingBody: Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education (KMK)
newRecords.summary: The key points treat digital media education and informatics education as cross-subject areas of Grundschule, based on the KMK competence framework. A separate Informatik subject in primary school is currently not planned. Bildungsstandards, including possible first standards for Sachunterricht, should take both areas into account.
newRecords.notes: The paper builds on the 'Vereinbarung zur Arbeit in der Grundschule' of 15.03.2024 and also covers teacher education. It states: 'Ein Unterrichtsfach Informatik in der Grundschule ist derzeit nicht vorgesehen.'

newRecords.title: Bildungsministerkonferenz adopts a declaration on handling social media in schools
newRecords.titleDe: Die Bildungsministerkonferenz beschließt eine Erklärung zum Umgang mit Social Media im schulischen Bereich
newRecords.summary: The Länder set three aims: raise awareness, build competence and protect pupils. Measures include covering social media in curricula across subjects, supporting parents, school rules on device use that protect the concentration and wellbeing of younger pupils, and teacher training on hate speech.
newRecords.notes: The text builds on the 2016 strategy and its 2021 supplement and welcomes a federal expert commission on child and youth protection in the digital world.

newRecords.title: Digitalpakt 2.0 starts: federal government and Länder release 5 billion euros for digital education
newRecords.titleDe: Der Digitalpakt 2.0 startet: Bund und Länder stellen 5 Milliarden Euro für digitale Bildung bereit
newRecords.issuingBody: Federal Ministry of Education, Family, Senior Citizens, Women and Youth (BMBFSFJ) and the Länder via the Bildungsministerkonferenz
newRecords.summary: After all Länder signed the administrative agreement, the federal education minister signed it too, which clears federal payments. It applies from 1 January 2026 for five years, with 5 billion euros split equally between the Bund and the Länder. Strand I funds school digital infrastructure; strand III adds 250 million euros of federal money for research.
newRecords.notes: The KMK press release is dated 01.09.2026. A BMBFSFJ press release of 19.08.2026 (https://www.bmbfsfj.bund.de/bmbfsfj/aktuelles/pressemitteilungen/digitalpakt-2-0-startet-am-1-september-293650) was also read and confirms the signatures. A joint declaration of 13.12.2024, adopted at the 2nd Bildungsministerkonferenz, named a total term of six years; the 2026 release gives five years.

newRecords.title: Bildungsministerkonferenz updates the KMK digital competence framework for artificial intelligence
newRecords.titleDe: Die Bildungsministerkonferenz beschließt die Aktualisierung des KMK-Kompetenzrahmens „Bildung in der digitalen Welt“ im Kontext Künstlicher Intelligenz
newRecords.summary: The update adds AI-related content to the six competence areas of the KMK framework, whose structure stays unchanged. It draws on the OECD and European Commission AI Literacy Framework, whose final version appeared in 2026, and uses four orientation terms for AI competence.
newRecords.notes: The four orientation terms are 'Mit KI bewusst umgehen', 'KI kreativ anwenden', 'KI gezielt einsetzen' and 'KI aktiv mitgestalten'. This decision is twelve days old at the time of research, so later corrections on the KMK site are possible.

newLinks.rationale: In 2005 Judge Jones ruled the Dover intelligent-design policy unconstitutional and found intelligent design to be a relabeled form of creationism. The ruling shows how evolution teaching is protected in US classrooms, the setting for this strand's content.

In 1989 California's Curriculum Commission endorsed a Science Framework that made evolution one of four central organizing themes. A state treating evolution as a unifying idea for science teaching parallels the role this strand has in Bio-Core.

This Florida record names the 2008 standard SC.912.L.15 (Diversity and Evolution of Living Organisms, grades 9-12) as an informal crosswalk target for this strand's natural selection and adaptation content. The record itself calls the mapping informal.

Tennessee's 2012 law shields teachers who critique the 'scientific weaknesses' of theories that cause debate, and it names biological evolution among them. It contrasts with a strand that teaches natural selection as a full explanatory model.

In late 2007 at least 12 Florida county school boards passed resolutions urging the State Board to revise draft standards over how evolution is presented as fact. This is local pushback against the kind of content this strand teaches.

The US Supreme Court held in 1968 that a state cannot ban the teaching of evolution, because the ban rested on one religious doctrine. It is the federal baseline for teaching the evolution content this strand covers.

In 1970 the Mississippi Supreme Court struck down its state's anti-evolution law, reasoning that Epperson had already settled the question. Mississippi and Arkansas were the only two states with such teaching bans left in 1968.

In 1987 the Supreme Court struck down a Louisiana law requiring 'creation science' alongside evolution, finding its purpose was to advance a religious view about the creation of humankind. It sets a limit on competing origin accounts in science class.

Tennessee's 1973 law required biology textbooks to give equal emphasis to the Genesis account and to carry a disclaimer about evolution's status as scientific fact. Courts struck it down in 1975. It contrasts with this strand's science-based account of diversity.

Dover's 2004 policy told students about 'gaps/problems in Darwin's theory' and offered intelligent design as an alternative explanation of the origin of life. It contrasts with this strand's evolutionary account of species and diversity.

This record traces the US evolution-education conflict from Tennessee's 1925 Butler Act through later 'academic freedom' laws, across several states and legal mechanisms. It gives the policy background for teaching this strand's content.

Bayern publishes a separate Fachlehrplan for each Jahrgangsstufe (for example Biologie 8 and Biologie 9), with no combined grade band. Bio-Core groups content into four bands (K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12), so the grain of the two plans differs.

Tennessee's 2022 science standards include a dedicated strand on Heredity, Inheritance and Variation of Traits (LS3) beside Biological Change (LS4). That heredity strand covers the same ground as this strand.

Per reviewers at public-comment sessions, Florida's 2026 draft high-school life-science standards lack gene flow and genetic drift. This substrand teaches allele-frequency change and the role of drift at the same level, so the draft stands in contrast.

Florida's 2008 benchmark SC.912.L.15.1 asks students to explain how evolution is supported by the fossil record and molecular biology, among other lines. It matches this substrand's indicator on judging common ancestry against several independent lines of evidence.

Tennessee benchmark BIO1.LS4.1 has students analyze data showing that common ancestry and evolution are supported by multiple lines of evidence, such as DNA sequences and the fossil record. It is close to this substrand's indicator on evaluating a common-ancestry claim.

Pennsylvania's 2022 standards include benchmark 3.1.9-12.S, in the strand Evidence of Common Ancestry and Diversity, on communicating that common ancestry and evolution rest on multiple lines of empirical evidence. It targets the same high-school skill as this substrand.

Sachsen-Anhalt's Sekundarschule Biologie plan for grades 9/10 asks students to show shared structures of organisms as a result of phylogenetic development, with the descent of humans as the example. The record compares this with the Gymnasium's grades 11/12.

This cross-state comparison puts human-evolution content in Thüringen at Klasse 10 and in Sachsen and Sachsen-Anhalt at the upper grades 11/12. It shows where three states place the phylogeny and evidence topics this substrand covers.

Thüringen's Regelschule plan for grades 9/10 has students explain the descent of modern humans with a simplified hominid cladogram and the evidence for reconstructing it. The record notes this content is guaranteed only on the Realschulabschluss track.

Per reviewers, Florida's 2026 draft middle-school standards mention natural selection without an explicit evolution framing. The record bears on how a grades 6-8 treatment of natural selection is named, which is the focus of this substrand.

This informal crosswalk maps Tennessee's Biological Change strands in grade 8 (8.LS4) and Biology I (BIO1.LS4) to Bio-Core's natural selection content. The grade 8 part falls inside this substrand's band.

Pennsylvania benchmark 3.1.9-12.T asks students to explain evolution through four factors, including heritable variation and the proliferation of better-surviving organisms. Bio-Core teaches this four-part model at grades 6-8, earlier than the standard does.

Tennessee benchmark BIO1.LS4.3 asks students to analyze how natural selection depends on heritable genetic variation and differential survival. These match the components of this substrand's four-part mechanism.

The C3 Framework guides states revising their social studies standards, with civics and history among its fields and an inquiry approach to teaching. As a K-12 civics reference it is a candidate comparison for this strand.

The Roadmap is a K-12 framework for history and civic education built around seven themes, offered as a starting point for standards and lessons. Its civic side can be compared with how this strand builds from groups to institutions.

The 2018 KMK recommendation treats the school as a place where democracy is taught and practised and names the Beutelsbach Consensus and its controversy principle. It gives a national German statement of civic aims to compare with this strand.

The SWK statement calls for shared competence goals and continuous Politik and Geschichte teaching from primary school to the end of Sekundarstufe I, with democracy education in all subjects. That span overlaps most of this strand's grade range.

The C3 Framework covers geography and history alongside civics and economics and organizes teaching around inquiry. Its history and geography parts can be compared with this strand's work on why societies differ and change.

The revised Grades 9-12 framework places Participation in Government and Civics and Economics in grade 12. This final-year course is a candidate counterpart for this substrand's work on formal institutions and incentives.

The Abitur requirements for Sozialkunde/Politik name political maturity and the capacity for democracy as aims and build on four competences, among them analysis and judgement. They give a German upper-secondary endpoint to compare with this substrand.

The revised Grades 9-12 framework sets Global History and Geography for grades 9 and 10 and United States History and Government for grade 11. These history courses are candidate places to compare with this substrand's work on explaining large-scale change.

Sachsen's grade-11 Gemeinschaftskunde unit on social structure and social change cross-references geography topics on population development and demographic change. It is a German upper-secondary case of teaching social change.

Five organizations released a K-12 framework of core computer science concepts and practices that describes how understanding grows over time. That growth-over-time design parallels this strand's K-2 to 9-12 progression.

CSTA published revised K-12 computer science standards aligned to the 2016 framework, updating its first comprehensive set from 2011. As a full K-12 standards set it is a direct comparison point for this strand's grade bands.

CSTA's 2026 PK-12 standards were finalized by 25 writers from 18 states and start at pre-kindergarten. This strand starts at K-2, so the pre-K years have no counterpart in it, while the K-12 span lets the two sets be compared band by band.

California's first K-12 computer science standards cover core concepts such as algorithms and programming and practices such as creating computational artifacts. These are the central topics of this strand across its bands.

Informatik in three states centers on a Modellieren competency. In Sachsen (Klassenstufen 7-10) pupils build models, then implement and test them. That matches this strand's focus on building and testing models and simulations.

The Modellieren und Implementieren competency also appears in Sachsen's Oberschule Informatik (7-10) and Sachsen-Anhalt's new Sekundarschule Informatik (5-8). It shows modelling as a core aim of lower secondary computing, as in this strand.

Sachsen's compulsory Gymnasium Informatik (Klassenstufen 7-10) has pupils implement, test, evaluate and revise their own solutions. The testing and revising step is close to the testing work in this 6-8 part.

Executive Order 14277 calls for online K-12 AI literacy resources and a White House task force on AI education. This strand's grade 9-12 part compares machine learning with other systems, so the AI literacy goal overlaps with it.
The order gives priority to high school AI courses. This 9-12 part compares machine learning, search and distributed systems, so it covers the same school stage and the same subject area.

The Bildungsministerkonferenz update adds AI content to the six KMK competence areas and draws on the OECD and European Commission AI literacy framework. This 9-12 part on machine learning is the closest part of the Core for AI content.

The KMK key points treat informatics education as a cross-subject area of Grundschule and currently plan no separate Informatik subject there. This frames how step-by-step work for the youngest pupils could be offered in German primary schools.

The KMK key points place informatics education in primary school as a cross-subject area, with no separate subject planned, and ask that Bildungsstandards take it into account. This frames where this grades 3-5 part could sit in Germany.

The Länder's 2026 declaration on social media aims to build pupils' competence and protect them, and calls for covering social media in curricula across subjects. This part uses a social media platform as its example of a shaped information environment.

Thüringen's Regelschule Informatik elective for grades 9 and 9/10 has students describe the history of information and communication technology and take a position on the chances and risks of informatics systems. It fits this part's technology and information-environment focus.

California's Board of Education adopted a 1989 policy limiting the science curriculum to 'observable facts and testable hypotheses'. It states the testability standard that this strand teaches students to apply to their own guesses and to scientific ideas.

This draft German principle proposes organizing interdisciplinary teaching around one integrating question, what it means to be human, so that linking subjects has a shared object of inquiry. This strand pulls evolutionary and cultural concepts into one shared vocabulary.

Pennsylvania's 2022 high school life science standards ask students to construct an evidence-based explanation that evolution results from four factors, including heritable variation. They give the biology reference point for this part's comparison of selection across domains.

Tennessee's 2022 Biology I benchmarks ask students to analyze data showing that natural selection is influenced by population growth potential and heritable genetic variation. This is the state's biological definition of selection, which this part sets beside the other three.

Sachsen's Oberschule Biologie plan for grade 10 lists the stages of human evolution and, in the same learning area, cultural evolution with language and cultures. It shows a state biology course naming cultural evolution next to the biological case.

Three German states center Informatik on modeling. The Sachsen text for grades 7 to 10 has students develop models, then test and revise their solution, a cycle that fits this part's focus on improving an idea through small changes.

California's Curriculum Commission endorsed a 1989 Science Framework making evolution one of four central organizing themes. This strand organizes content across domains around one shared pattern of variation and selection.
